content: Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) was compared to cytology (ASCUS) followed by colposcopic impression and biopsy when indicated. The outcomes of these screening and treatment strategies were evaluated for patient-important outcomes, with data presented per 100,000 patients. 1. Mortality from cervical cancer: VIA combined with cold knife conization (CKC) resulted in 1,108 deaths, while VIA with loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) or cryotherapy each resulted in 1,195 deaths. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC resulted in 783 deaths, with LEEP in 908 deaths, and with cryotherapy in 909 deaths. In the absence of screening, mortality was significantly higher at 4,350 deaths. 2. Cervical cancer incidence: VIA with CKC led to 2,151 cases, while VIA with LEEP or cryotherapy each resulted in 1,673 cases. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC resulted in 1,097 cases, with LEEP in 1,273 cases, and with cryotherapy in 1,273 cases. Without screening, the incidence was 6,075 cases. 3. CIN 2+ recurrence: VIA with CKC resulted in 319 recurrences, while VIA with LEEP or cryotherapy each resulted in 999 and 22 recurrences, respectively. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC resulted in 386 recurrences, with LEEP in 186 recurrences, and with cryotherapy in 186 recurrences. Without screening, there were 575 recurrences. 4. Undetected CIN 2+ (false negatives): VIA with CKC resulted in 23,000 undetected cases, while VIA with LEEP or cryotherapy resulted in 16,000 undetected cases. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC, LEEP, or cryotherapy had no undetected cases. 5. Major bleeding: VIA with CKC resulted in 4,205 cases of major bleeding, while VIA with LEEP or cryotherapy resulted in 539 and 81 cases, respectively. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC resulted in 721 cases, with LEEP in 190 cases, and with cryotherapy in 28 cases. No major bleeding occurred in the absence of treatment. 6. Premature delivery: VIA with CKC resulted in 788 cases of premature delivery, while VIA with LEEP or cryotherapy resulted in 602 and 649 cases, respectively. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC resulted in 601 cases, with LEEP in 536 cases, and with cryotherapy in 553 cases. Without screening, there were 500 cases. 7. Infertility: No data were identified regarding the risk of infertility following treatment for CIN 2+. 8. Major infections: VIA with CKC resulted in 721 cases of major infections, while VIA with LEEP or cryotherapy resulted in 212 and 32 cases, respectively. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC resulted in 75 cases, with LEEP in 107 cases, and with cryotherapy in 11 cases. No major infections occurred in untreated cases. 9. Minor infections: VIA with CKC resulted in 2,239 cases of minor infections, while VIA with LEEP or cryotherapy resulted in 1,440 and 1,547 cases, respectively. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC resulted in 787 cases, with LEEP in 506 cases, and with cryotherapy in 544 cases. No minor infections occurred in untreated cases. 10. Unnecessarily treated cases (false positives): VIA with CKC resulted in 162,000 unnecessary treatments, while VIA with LEEP or cryotherapy resulted in no unnecessary treatments. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC, LEEP, or cryotherapy also resulted in no unnecessary treatments. 11. Cancer detected at first-time screening: VIA with CKC detected 3,168 cancers, while VIA with LEEP or cryotherapy detected 4,794 and 0 cancers, respectively. Cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC detected 128 cancers. The evidence quality for these outcomes was generally very low due to limitations in study design, indirectness, and imprecision. The expert panel recommended a screen-and-treat strategy using HPV testing followed by cryotherapy (or LEEP if cryotherapy is not feasible) over HPV testing followed by colposcopy and biopsy. This recommendation was based on the balance of benefits and harms, resource implications, and patient preferences. However, the addition of colposcopy requires more resources, training, and follow-up visits, which may not be feasible in resource-limited settings.
